# Writing the skills

The curator directs this restoration and reads every skill with human eyes. The writer edits a skill, a part is a file under its `references/`, and the record is the project's memory under `explorations/`. The register is Simplified Technical English (ASD-STE100), about halfway. Each principle gives its reason, then a text he marked and the text he accepted.

## 1. Define a term before you use it, and use plain words everywhere else

A reader new to the repository has only the skill, its brief and its training. A word with a meaning that the record gave it (a defect's "home", a "stop" that does not stop, "corpus") tells it nothing or the wrong thing. Where its training holds a near thing, name it ("as LLVM's lit does"): one clause corrects an assumption where a paragraph would not.
- Marked: "In every report, give each defect's home, ..."
- Accepted: "In your report, list each defect that you found, with the test or ledger row that records it."

## 2. Put the concepts first, as a dictionary, then the procedures in the order that the work meets them

A chain of do's and don'ts cannot be held in mind; a concept named once (an area, building, exploring, a point to report) makes each procedure short and tells the reader when to switch. A glossary entry is the term, then a noun phrase with no article. A comment marks a problem area: fix it at its paragraph or section, with the whole skill in mind.
- Marked: "- The base is the commit that your work starts from."
- Accepted: "**base**" / ": Commit that your work starts from."

## 3. Every sentence tells the reader what to do or a fact it needs to do it; cut the rest

Every agent pays for every token, and a sentence that changes nothing hides the ones that do: a slogan (a decision's title copied from the record), a step the agent takes anyway, a rule it cannot act on, a rule against a failure that never happened, a rule its system prompt gives, a back reference, a provenance word.
- Marked: "1. Read your brief. 2. Load the parts below that your task touches. [...] 4. Do the work."
- Accepted: "Load the parts below that your task touches before you run the query of the record that your brief gives. The parts give the words [...]"

## 4. State a rule for exactly the cases where it holds, and bound it to the agent's brief and its own work

A wider rule sends the agent to do what cannot be done: a test for a specification edit, a search through other agents' transcripts, a question to the curator. An absolute ("never wipe the caches") is wrong in the cases it did not name. Authority reaches an agent through its brief alone, and what a role or a workflow does belongs there, not in the skill.
- Marked: "Before you build or run something, look for its result on record. If the record or another agent's transcript holds the result [...], cite that result"
- Accepted: "Reuse each result of a build, a suite, a stage of the gate or a test that your brief cites or that your own work ran. Cite it."

Misapplied: cutting the default for a silent brief ("If it says nothing, commit your own files as you go") leaves the agent with no action. A cut never removes a default.

A prohibition hides the mechanism it protects ("Do not ask the curator anything" hid how a question reaches him), and a compressed rule loses its purpose. A sentence that carries a list, a quoted title and a pointer cannot be held in mind; three short ones can.
- Marked: "Change one variable per step."
- Accepted: "When you probe or debug, change one thing at a time, so that each result has one cause."

The curator reads for duplication at every scale: a word written twice, a fact said twice, a paragraph where a sentence does. A longer rewrite is a regression, however clear.
- Marked: "Do not pipe `ant` through `tail`: `tail` prints only after the command ends, and only its last lines. If the Bash tool's time limit stops the run first, you see nothing [...]"

374	
375	Retain Markdown and permanent F-identifiers. Refine the existing entry form; do not introduce a database or require every entry to fill repetitive labelled fields.
376	
377	Each entry should communicate:
378	
379	1. **Current claim and scope.** What is established, on which execution path, library, call form or other relevant conditions. The title must not imply a broader claim than the body supports.
380	2. **Consequence and limits.** What a worker can safely conclude or do, with exceptions and unresolved uncertainty kept beside the claim. Include consequences only when they matter.
381	3. **Evidence and route to detail.** The supporting test, measurement, source reading or report section. Distinguish observed behaviour from code inspection or an inference. A missing automated test is not itself a defect if other evidence is honestly identified.

Link to the owning current count rather than duplicating a count that changes at every landing.
384	
385	A FACTS entry may record an implementation choice made under a default. It must distinguish that fact from a curator-approved ruling. POSITIONS owns the ruling; history owns its origin.
386

388

391	| Criterion | Pass condition |
392	|---|---|
393	| Scope | Title and body agree on the path, conditions and limits; the statement does not generalize beyond its support. |
394	| Present meaning | The reader can identify the current property, or the explicitly bounded historical observation, without reconstructing a batch's work. |
395	| Evidence | The stated support can be found and supports the retained claim; uncertainty and the kind of evidence are accurately represented. |
396	| Comprehension | Given normal language prerequisites, a reader can restate the finding and its consequence. Subjects, referents and technical terms are unambiguous. |
397	| Ownership | The entry has one independently maintainable subject; unrelated repairs, chronology and duplicated current counts do not obscure it. |
398	| Consistency | Relevant linked or same-subject entries agree, or their different scopes or unresolved conflict are explicit. |

403

405	- **Reword:** supported meaning is sound, but presentation or scope wording fails.

424

426	
427	- **Rung workers:** provide precise findings, conditions, evidence and implications in their reports and `record.md`. No added prose-polishing workflow.
428	- **Gather:** incorporate the findings without losing scope or provenance.

430	- **Coordinator:** own the guidance and verify that the pass occurred. Delegate the writing through the existing process; this need not become another task the coordinator personally performs in full.
431

Do not add another full-record audit after every landing.

443

- **Rung workers:** provide precise findings, conditions, evidence and implications in their reports and `record.md`. No added prose-polishing workflow.
- **Gather:** incorporate the findings without losing scope or provenance.
- **Record pass:** produce the final readable entries and check their scope, evidence and related statements. The coordinator's instructions assign this to the batch commit stage, and to the coordinator after a lone worker.
- **Coordinator:** own the guidance and verify that the pass occurred. Delegate the writing through the existing process; this need not become another task the coordinator personally performs in full.

Align the rung brief's request for “finished prose” with the worker skill: request complete findings, while making the record pass responsible for final editorial wording.

Put the schema clarification and assessment criteria in `.claude/skills/coordinator/references/record.md`. Ensure the actual batch stage brief carries that guidance, rather than assuming the descriptive skill text alone causes it to happen. The full pass is a one-time repair of the accumulated record; subsequent landings apply the same criteria to new, changed and affected related entries. Do not add another full-record audit after every landing.

For routine acceptance, keep the central question short:

> Can a reader identify what is established, under which conditions, and what it means for the work, without reconstructing what the batch changed?

The corresponding POSITIONS question remains about faithful communication of the curator's ruling. The shared register helps both; their evidence and ownership requirements remain distinct.

## Review limits

This review sampled Revival and its sources. It did not reread the whole file, audit FACTS or POSITIONS, inspect transcripts, run builds, or test the numerical claims anew. Growth measurements are attributed to the existing scout report.

<!-- The clarity workflow: rewrite POSITIONS or FACTS entries so that each reads on its own, with a cold read and a fidelity check, as a Workflow run; how to run it and what to do with its output. -->

# The clarity workflow

`record-clarity.js` rewrites record entries so that a reader who knows the language, but never saw the conversation or the batch behind an entry, can tell what it says. It is the process of the clarity pilot of 2026-10-22 (`positions-audit/clarity/`, ten POSITIONS entries, approved and applied at `6b560762f`), run as a Workflow, in the shape of the `fortress-repo` skill rewrite of 2026-10-08 (Workflow run `wf_185878c8-0fb`: writers, cold readers, a fix round). Its standard is Astra's review, `explorations/reviews/revival-record-synthesis.md`.

## What runs, for each chunk of about ten entries

1. **Assess** (FACTS only): Astra's rubric over every entry (`assess.md`); a disposition each: keep, reword, reorganize or investigate. Only reword and reorganize go on.
2. **Write**: the stream's headless Opus writer (`writer-stream.sh`, the skill writer's standing brief) with `writer.md`. For POSITIONS its evidence is the provenance audit's, by `entries.py`; for FACTS, the assessment and each entry's cited sources. A Sonnet step only runs the command and waits (`wait.py`).
3. **Cold read**: an Opus reader with only the `fortress-repo` skill's core and area parts, never its revival part (`coldread.md`).
4. **Check**: fidelity against the sources, and the reader's answers against the source meaning (`check.md`).
5. **Fix**: the writer's second round (`fix.md`), in the same stream, so it resumes the session that wrote the chunk with its evidence in the cache.
6. **Reread**: a second cold read of the fixed entries.
7. **Judge**: once, per entry, apply or hold (`judge.md`), so that no chunk loops; it writes `final.apply` and `queue.md`.

**The writer stream.** One headless Opus session per Workflow run takes its chunks in turn (`flock`), resumed while its context stays under 400K tokens written and its cache is warm (under 50 minutes idle), and started fresh otherwise. In the pilot its fix round wrote 61K tokens, where a fresh writer would read everything again. A Workflow runs at most two agents at once on this machine: run several side by side, each with its own stream.

## Running it

    Workflow({ scriptPath: '/home/user/fortress/explorations/coordinator/tools/record-clarity/record-clarity.js',
               args: { kind: 'positions' | 'facts', out: '/abs/folder/', stream: 'name', chunks: [{ name: 'c1', entries: ['P-7', 'P-8'] }] } })

`from: 'judge'` runs only the judge, on chunks written before the judge existed.

Each chunk's files land in `out` + its name: `proposals.md`, `clean.txt`, `proposals.apply`, `concepts.md`, `cold-read.md`, `check.md`, `cold-read-2.md`, `judgement.md`, `final.apply`, `queue.md`, the writer's logs, and for FACTS `assessment.md`. Resume a killed run with the same script path, `resumeFromRunId` and the same args, byte for byte.

## After a chunk

The coordinator's part is mechanical:
- apply the judge's `final.apply` on a copy of the record, `record.py check --base`, then on `main`, and commit the record with the chunk's files;
- file `queue.md` in `review-queue.md` (a worker, for several chunks at once);
- merge `concepts.md` into the concepts list that the orientation workflow reads.

POSITIONS entries need the provenance audit's evidence first: for entries it has not traced, run the mining workflow (`positions-audit/README.md`).

# FACTS chunk f0: the rewrite

The base is `main` at `df0728b81`, as in `assessment.md`; the fix round read at `30ee7ae4b`, whose library, ledger and gate files are the base's (`check.md`). The assessment keeps F-261 and F-262, so this file holds the other three: F-151 (reword), F-263 and F-264 (reorganize). Each entry's sources are the assessment's and the check's citations, read again for the sentence that cites them. A section number is that of the report named. Concepts that the entries use and that every worker needs are in `concepts.md`.

The fix round changed what `check.md` marks, and the readings that `cold-read.md` could not resolve:
- F-151: which declarations need `Number`'s exclusion, corrected; the library named; the default's wording; the plain array said as a run-time result; two claims added from the sources.
- F-263: the compiled path's negative power narrowed to `ZZ32`'s and its bases; the `IntLiteral` value, the exponent beyond 64 bits and row 523's failure said plainly.
- F-264: the subscripts' cast put back on the sub-array that they pass to `Col` and `Row`; the walk claim at landing narrowed to its measurement; the factory branches and the five bodies that need no cast named.

The three entries hold 3,179 characters in the record and 5,905 here: F-151 617 to 1,850, F-263 1,359 to 1,962, F-264 1,203 to 2,093. The growth is the words that say what each pointer holds, the names that replace the batches' short forms, the conditions that the old text left to the reader, and the fix round's corrections and named lists. `record.py apply` of `proposals.apply` on a scratch clone of the record at `30ee7ae4b`, then `record.py check --base df0728b81` on it: 0 failures.

## F-151

> - F-151 **In the interpreter's library, `Vector`, `Matrix` and their factories and operators bound their element type by `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }`.** `Number` declares no arithmetic, so the compiled checker accepts the bodies' arithmetic only through `MultiplicativeRing[\T\]`. `Number` stays in the bound because its `comprises` clause lists every type below it, so an element type excludes `String`; the ring alone does not give that. That exclusion makes the four juxtapositions of a vector or a matrix with a scalar `T`, in either order, a valid overloading beside the library's juxtapositions with a `String`. `Number` also declares the `asFloat` that the vector norm calls. The eight number types meet the bound. `Number` itself and the numeral type `IntLiteral` do not, since neither is a ring at its own type. # Rung G, climb batch 6.5: generics at run time on the compiled path

problem: six compiled-path failures, each re-captured on the base before any edit: row 417's first-load race at four threads (explorations/compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/probes/threads-before.txt:10), row 419's task (probes/junit-before.txt:128), row 420 (:151), the renamed-arm and ZZ32 dispatch defects (:71, :109), row 351 at the typecase and catch sites (:6, :174) and row 426 through the compiler library's cast (explorations/compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/probes/junit-before.txt:25)

precedent: row 419 copies forFnExpr's own closure device (ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/codegen/CodeGen.java:3479-3489); row 351 copies forLocalVarDecl's local and nested scope (:3959-3962, :4018-4027) and conditionallyCastParameter's cast (:6463-6467); row 417 takes the lock of the JDK method it overrides (explorations/compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/probes/jdk-loadclass-javap.txt:2-9), the team's check-again-under-the-table's-lock (ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/RttiTupleMap.java:148-157); the dispatch change is the measured patch (explorations/compile-ladder/plan-6.5/probes/dispatch/callsite-rebased.patch:1-119)
deviation: the dispatch patch without its `-Dprobe.scope` switch and its `skip` variant (ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/compiler/OverloadSet.java:1338-1370); row 419's patch plus the deletion of the TO DO line it answers (CodeGen.java:1633); the lock wraps the old body in a helper rather than re-indenting it, and `history` is still written before `defineClass` (ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:178-211); the identity functions' ZZ32 and RR64 branches take a typed binding where the answer-7 text passed a numeral (Library/FortressLibrary.fss:3126-3128)

Every capture named below is in `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/probes/` unless a path says otherwise. The harness refused this rung's write of this file; the gather writes it from the structured result.

## 1. What is fixed

All six, on the compiled path:

1. **Row 417, the first-load race.** `InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` now runs under `getClassLoadingLock(name)`, the lock the JDK's own `ClassLoader.loadClass` takes and this override had dropped. `FirstLoadThreadsRungG` fails 5 of 5 compiled runs at `FORTRESS_THREADS=4` on the base (`threads-before.txt:10-14`, `NullPointerException ... "cl" is null`) and passes 5 of 5 after (`threads-after.txt:10-14`); both pass at one thread. Rung Z's `ZsThreadsT`, `ZsThreadsS`, `ZsThreads` and the control `ZsThreadsLit` pass 5 of 5 at both counts (`threads-zs-after.txt`), and a 24-instantiation widening passes 5 of 5 (`FirstLoad24.fss`, `threads-24-after.txt`).
2. **Row 419, a task in a generic declaration.** The measured 13-line patch: `delegate` makes the task class generic over the task's free static parameters, as `forFnExpr` does for a closure. `NatRtTask` (promoted from `XXXNatRtTask`) passes.
3. **Row 420, a generic method building over two parameter sets.** Its site is row 419's: the method's `||` operands are run as a task, and the task class was not generic. Disassembled on the base, the method template `H☝m⟦☝,U,T⟧` builds its second operand in the non-generic `ZrMethNoClosureT$task0`, which names `U`. Two controls on the base settle it (`row420-cause-before.txt`): the method's own parameter alone, in two task operands, fails the same way (`MethOneParTask`, `U$RTTIc`), and both parameters with no task operand pass (`MethBothNoTask`, `stringzz32`). Row 419's fix closes it: `NatRtMethBoth` (promoted, with a third assertion for `MethOneParTask`'s shape) passes. The row's "both parameters" reading was the controls' shape, not the cause.
4. **A generic arm naming its static parameters differently from its template dispatcher.** The measured call-site change. `DispatchRenamedArmRungG` and `DispatchSwappedArmRungG` (the plan's `ScopeArmsLegal` and `ScopeAlpha2`) pass.
5. **A `ZZ32` instantiation spelled at run time.** Avoided on template dispatchers by the same change, which names the arm at the dispatcher's own parameters instead of reading them off the value. `DispatchZZ32ArmRungG` (`ScopeZZ32Sub`) passes. The two spellings remain (section 9).
6. **Row 351, a clause's bound name, and row 426.** `forTypecase` binds a named clause's value as a local for the clause body, and `forTry` binds the catch name the same way. `TypecaseBindRungG`, `ArrowClauseBindRungG` (`andCondCombine`'s shape), `CastBindRungG`, `WitnessIdentityRungG` and `ClauseBindingRungB` (promoted from `XXXClauseBindingRungB`) pass. Row 426 was row 351: the compiled `cast[\T\]` matched and then read its clause name as a missing top-level object. `cast-template-javap.txt` shows it: before, `getstatic fortress/CompilerLibrary$y.ONLY` (`:11`); after, `checkcast T`, `astore_1`, `aload_1` (`:35-37`). Its numeral half, `cast[\ZZ32\](0)` throwing, is the specification's answer (section 4). Answer 7's identity functions now pass values of type `T` through `cast` in their `ZZ32` and `RR64` branches. A named clause or a `catch` inside a `do … also` arm whose body then reads a captured variable still fails verification. A local in a task body takes `this`'s slot (row 497). A `catch` there also meets row 322's mechanism (`explorations/compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/probes/skeptic/clause-in-task.txt:33-34`, `:50`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/probes/skeptic/clause-in-task-split.txt:62`, `:95`, `explorations/compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/probes/skeptic/try-in-arm.txt:41`).

What remains is recorded, not fixed: the dispatch change's remainder (generic dotted methods, home 2; a dispatcher that is not a template, home 3), sections 9 and 10.

## 12. Decisions, each with the ways not taken

- **The lock's shape.** Candidates:
  - `synchronized (getClassLoadingLock(name))` around the whole of `loadClass`, which is the loader's own monitor. Taken.
  - The same with `registerAsParallelCapable`, one lock per name.
  - A lock only in `loadClosureClass`.
  - A `ConcurrentHashMap` of futures per name.

  The monitor is the lock the JVM already holds when it resolves a class through a loader that is not parallel-capable, and it is what the JDK's own `loadClass` takes. Explicit loads (`loadClosureClass`, `getRTTIclass`, the union instantiation) were the only ones running without it. Taking it adds no lock order the implicit loads do not already have: a generation step that initialises another class under the monitor, as `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/MethodInstantiater.java:274` can, already does so on every implicit load. Per-name locks would admit two loads each holding one name's lock while generating a class that needs the other's; the JDK leaves them off unless a loader opts in. A lock in `loadClosureClass` alone leaves the other two explicit callers racing. Futures would change the loader's structure for no gain the measurement can see.
- **Where `history` is written.** Left before `defineClass`. Under the lock no other thread can see the name before its class is defined. Moving the write would change what the same thread does if generation re-enters the loader for the name it is generating, which it does not today by reading, and every single-thread run would need re-measuring for no gain. The pre-existing behaviour after a failed load, where the name stays in `history` and a later load of it returns null (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:189-193`), is unchanged; by reading, not measured.
- **Binding a catch name always.** The grammar makes the name mandatory (`try.tex:22`), and the specification binds it (`:56-60`), so every catch clause's code changes: `getValue`, a cast and a store in place of a pop. The prelude has no `catch`, so no library class moves. The other way, binding only a name the body reads, needs a free-variable test at each clause and saves three instructions.
- **Binding a typecase clause's name only when it has one.** Clauses without a name pop as before, which is why only `cast`'s template changed in the prelude.
- **The identity functions' values of type `T`.** Two ways were on file:
  - A typed binding, `v: ZZ32 = 0` then `cast[\T\](v)`, which converts a numeral by coercion on the compiled path and keeps walk's value as it is (FACTS.md, "Under walk, the interpreter converts by coercion at its three kinds of type check", FACTS.md:110). Taken, in the two branches that passed a numeral.
  - A checker refinement that binds `T` inside a witness branch (`explorations/reviews/sum-replacement-judgement.md` section 7, check 3), which is Scala and not this rung's. Not taken.

  `typed` would not do: the compiled path has no `forAsExpr`. The six branches that pass a function's result (`widen`, `unsigned`, `big`, `Ratio`, `narrow`) are unchanged. They have values of their type under walk, where a numeral is a `ZZ32`, and in the compiled checker's reading of the one library, where `IntLiteral` extends `ZZ32` (`ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fsi:117`). They do not over the compiled prelude, where a numeral reaches `ZZ32`'s and `NN32`'s `widen` by coercion alone and the checker's pick differed between two compiles (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-6.5/merged-review/witness-identity-gate.txt`, `compile-ladder/climb-batch-6.5/judge-repair/witness-suite-javap.txt`). So `WitnessIdentityRungG` widens a typed `ZZ32` since the judge's repair (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-6.5/JUDGE-review.md` section 2).
- **Row 420's fix is row 419's.** No separate edit was made; the row closes with 419, its cause located and gated.
- **Home 3, not home 2, for a dispatcher that is not a template.** The batch record plans home 2 for both remainders "where the rung shows it failing" (`explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-6.5.md:188`). For generic dotted methods the rung took it (`XXXDispatchMethodArmRungG`). For a dispatcher that is not a template the alternative was an `XXX` test asserting only that the call does not throw and answers one of the two declarations. It was not taken, because the chapter as committed forbids the pair (`Specification/basic/overloading.tex:102-105`), so no passage says which answer a test should hold, and the grep of section 9 finds none; home 3, the probes and row 496.
- **Two more compiled tests than the brief named.** `WitnessIdentityRungG` is answer 7's identity shape in the compiler's world. It is the judgement's check 3, `zeroOf[\RR64\]()` through a repaired `cast`, now gated. `XXXDispatchMethodArmRungG` is the remainder's home 2.

Rung Z's `ZsThreadsT`, `ZsThreadsS`, `ZsThreads` and the control `ZsThreadsLit` pass 5 of 5 at both counts (`threads-zs-after.txt`), and a 24-instantiation widening passes 5 of 5 (`FirstLoad24.fss`, `threads-24-after.txt`).
2. **Row 419, a task in a generic declaration.** The measured 13-line patch: `delegate` makes the task class generic over the task's free static parameters, as `forFnExpr` does for a closure. `NatRtTask` (promoted from `XXXNatRtTask`) passes.
3. **Row 420, a generic method building over two parameter sets.** Its site is row 419's: the method's `||` operands are run as a task, and the task class was not generic. Disassembled on the base, the method template `H☝m⟦☝,U,T⟧` builds its second operand in the non-generic `ZrMethNoClosureT$task0`, which names `U`. Two controls on the base settle it (`row420-cause-before.txt`): the method's own parameter alone, in two task operands, fails the same way (`MethOneParTask`, `U$RTTIc`), and both parameters with no task operand pass (`MethBothNoTask`, `stringzz32`). 6. **Row 351, a clause's bound name, and row 426.** `forTypecase` binds a named clause's value as a local for the clause body, and `forTry` binds the catch name the same way. `TypecaseBindRungG`, `ArrowClauseBindRungG` (`andCondCombine`'s shape), `CastBindRungG`, `WitnessIdentityRungG` and `ClauseBindingRungB` (promoted from `XXXClauseBindingRungB`) pass. ## 12. Decisions, each with the ways not taken

- **The lock's shape.** Candidates:
  - `synchronized (getClassLoadingLock(name))` around the whole of `loadClass`, which is the loader's own monitor. Taken.
  - The same with `registerAsParallelCapable`, one lock per name.
  - A lock only in `loadClosureClass`.
  - A `ConcurrentHashMap` of futures per name.

  The monitor is the lock the JVM already holds when it resolves a class through a loader that is not parallel-capable, and it is what the JDK's own `loadClass` takes. Explicit loads (`loadClosureClass`, `getRTTIclass`, the union instantiation) were the only ones running without it. Taking it adds no lock order the implicit loads do not already have: a generation step that initialises another class under the monitor, as `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/runtimeSystem/MethodInstantiater.java:274` can, already does so on every implicit load. Per-name locks would admit two loads each holding one name's lock while generating a class that needs the other's; the JDK leaves them off unless a loader opts in. A lock in `loadClosureClass` alone leaves the other two explicit callers racing. Futures would change the loader's structure for no gain the measurement can see.

Moving the write would change what the same thread does if generation re-enters the loader for the name it is generating, which it does not today by reading, and every single-thread run would need re-measuring for no gain. The pre-existing behaviour after a failed load, where the name stays in `history` and a later load of it returns null (`InstantiatingClassloader.java:189-193`), is unchanged; by reading, not measured.

object Vt[\T\](x: ZZ32) end
object A1 end

object A4 end
object A5 end
object A6 end
object A7 end
object A8 end

f[\T\](v: Vt[\T\]): ZZ32 = v.x
f(x: Any): ZZ32 = 0

mk(j: ZZ32): Any =
  if j = 0 then Vt[\A1\](1)
  elif j = 1 then Vt[\A2\](2)
  elif j = 2 then Vt[\A3\](3)
  elif j = 3 then Vt[\A4\](4)
  elif j = 4 then Vt[\A5\](5)
  elif j = 5 then Vt[\A6\](6)
  elif j = 6 then Vt[\A7\](7)

step(i: ZZ32): () = do

  atomic do sAcc := sAcc + a end
end

run(): () = do
  for i <- 0#800 do step(i) end
  if sAcc = 3600 then
    println("PASS")
  else
    println("FAIL: sum " sAcc " expected 3600, ledger row 417, Specification/basic/overloading.tex, section \"Overloading Resolution\"")

end

**The smallest run that reports the whole distance is that one JVM run**: one command (`run-all.sh <work-dir> build stage`), the twelve components with `FortressLibrary` first, whose target checks the twelve apis with every stage, then the other eleven with the apis checked the tracked way.

The `FortressLibrary` target alone reports 940 of the 1,527 and misses the other eleven components' 587; and it is the part that takes the time (two thirds of the run), so leaving out a small component saves seconds (`AnyType`, `TypeProxy`, `Stream` and `NatReflect` take under 3 s each in the one-JVM run).

# The distance to the switch-over, measured on the flat library

The terms are those of `switch-over-distance.md` ("Terms"): the count stage, the api and component layers, the early return, walk's setting and the compile path's setting, a distinct error. One more here:
- *Site*: an error's kind and location (file and line, two for a pair), with the lines of the 2026-09-26 tables carried to today's files by a line map (`compare-sites.py`). Two trees are compared by site because a message that lists candidate declarations changes when a candidate's type changes, while the obligation at the site does not.

## The answers

1. **Everything the checker reports, today: 1,736 distinct errors under walk's setting, 1,527 under the compile path's, against 2,523 and 2,359 on 2026-09-26.** The count stage reads 62, 3.6 % of the walk figure (5 % on 2026-09-26). The api layer went 551 → 223 (walk) and 628 → 297 (compile); the twelve components 1,972 → 1,513 and 1,731 → 1,230. Eight declarations crash the checker, from nine (§ 2).
2. **What went is the number tower's, and what stays is almost all of what the 2026-09-26 note listed as not the tower's.** Measured by site (walk): 986 sites went, 199 appeared, 1,537 stayed. ## 5. The distance stage for phase 3's gates

**One full run takes about 24 minutes on this machine as it was loaded, whichever way it is run.** The compile path's setting, the twelve components, every stage, memo off:
- as twelve JVMs (`check-compile`, the method above): 1,440 s, `FortressLibrary` 770 s, `RangeInternals` 305 s, the other ten 365 s;
- as one JVM with one private cache (`stage`, `DistanceMulti.java`, `r6-stage-compile.out`): 1,431 s, `FortressLibrary` 977 s, `RangeInternals` 258 s, the other ten 158 s, the rest start-up.
Load average 13 to 18 at the starts, with one to three other runs of this probe beside each and the overflow batch throughout; the two are not a comparison of the two ways. The same one-JVM run under walk's setting, started last (`stage-walk`, `r6-stage-walk.out`), took 850 s, `FortressLibrary` 587 s: load 14.8 at its start and 6.5 at its end, with no other run of this probe beside it after its second minute. So the stage costs between about 14 and 24 minutes on this machine, by its load; on an idle one, less, not measured.

**The smallest run that reports the whole distance is that one JVM run**: one command (`run-all.sh <work-dir> build stage`), the twelve components with `FortressLibrary` first, whose target checks the twelve apis with every stage, then the other eleven with the apis checked the tracked way.
- It reports what the twelve runs report, within the checker's run-to-run variation: 1,531 distinct errors against 1,527; every unit's count equal except `FortressLibrary`'s (api 195 → 196, component 643 → 646); the 23 errors that go and the 27 that appear are all of the variation's kind (which pair of `LEXICO`, `SQCAP` or `INVERSE` declarations is named, the order of a union's members in a message, the type a join infers for an array body); the same eight crashes and the same stage crash (`compare-stage-compile.txt`).
- Nothing smaller reports the whole distance. The `FortressLibrary` target alone reports 940 of the 1,527 and misses the other eleven components' 587; and it is the part that takes the time (two thirds of the run), so leaving out a small component saves seconds (`AnyType`, `TypeProxy`, `Stream` and `NatReflect` take under 3 s each in the one-JVM run).
- A report-only stage should compare by kind and unit, or by site (`compare-sites.py`), not by error: the variation moves a few errors of a run every time (1,527 against 1,531 here; 1,736 against 1,738 for the one-JVM run under walk's setting, `compare-stage-walk.txt`; 1,055 against 1,051 in the rung F control of § 1), always in the families named above, and the kind counts do not move except the components' type errors, by 2 to 4.
- The shadows are made from the tracked sources at every build, by text edits that must each match exactly once (`make-shadows.sh`, `r00-make-shadows.txt`), so a tracked edit that moves an anchor stops the build; there is no copied source to go stale silently, which is what the count stage's `#shadow` row guards.
- Code generation is not in it: § 3's per-declaration run adds about 8 minutes, § 4's dispatch run about 10, on this machine as loaded.

**Which setting the stage should run is open.** Answer 11 names the compile path's (`coordinator/POSITIONS.md`, 2026-09-26). Batch 7's Q1, default (a), would bound an unbounded type parameter by `Any`, and the switch-over would then take walk's bound for the compiled path (`coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-7.md` § 1, Q1). The compiled path would keep its compiled-expression desugaring, which code generation relies on for `case` and type ascriptions (`compiler/Desugarer.java:124`, `:141`; inferred that it is kept). That is a third setting, neither column of § 2: `-setting any` of `DistanceMulti.java`, bound `Any`, compiled-expression desugaring on. Measured once (`stage-any`, `r6-stage-any.out`, `errors-stage-any.txt`): **1,747 distinct errors**, walk's 1,736 and the compile path's 12 abstract-method errors of `FortressLibrary`'s component (inferred: from the compiled-expression desugaring's `AbstractDesugarer`, which marks a bodyless function abstract, `compiler/desugarer/AbstractDesugarer.java:40-46`), one export error fewer, the variance checker's stage crash on `Stream`, the rest the variation (`compare-walk-any.txt`). So under (a) the stage runs `stage-any`, and walk's column is within a dozen errors of it; under (b), `stage`. Both would double the stage.

**It finishes, and refuses 12 overload sets, from 131.** The run of § 3 with dispatch generation left on, under JFR, took 610 s: the checker and desugaring about 400 s, then code generation, dispatch generation included, from 10:49:57 to 10:53:26 UTC, about 210 s (`r3-dispatch.watch.txt`, `r3-dispatch.out`). The 119 tower sets and the 12 "Only handling some static args of generic types" (a size in an overload arm) are gone.
- Otherwise the declarations fare as in § 3: 325 emitted, 228 refused, the same 4 on declarations the checker passed (`r3-dispatch.classified.txt`).
- **Where the time goes** (`r3-dispatch.jfr-codegen.txt`, 16.0K samples in the code-generation window): 60 % of the samples reach the phase's own frame (JFR keeps 64 frames); 37 % have the exclusion test `TypeAnalyzer.pExc` on the stack, 33 % its comprises-clause check; 31 % the overloading oracle's `lteq`; 24 % `CodeGen.generateTopLevelOverloads`, dispatch generation proper; self time is 78 % the Scala tree walker `Walker.walk`.

# Can the compiler just use `FortressLibrary`?

Pavol's question, verbatim:

> I still don't get why the library needs to be rewritten for the compiler,
> other than your guess that the interpreter's standard library would not pass
> the type checker. What's specific to bytecode generation in there? Couldn't
> the path forward be just to use the FortressLibrary for the compiler as
> well? What breaks and when?

Answered by trying it. Every command and its full output is in this directory;
`run-all.sh` lists them in order. Host: JDK 25.0.3, `source experiment/env.sh`
(`FORTRESS_THREADS=1`, `-Xmx4g -Xss64m`), tree at HEAD, caches wiped and the
compiler library chain rebuilt from scratch first (106 s, `01-library-chain.out`).
Nothing outside this directory was modified.

**The short answer.** Almost nothing in `FortressLibrary.fss` is about bytecode
generation. 4.7% of it (211 of 4,518 lines) is native bindings, and those are
the *only* genuinely codegen-specific thing in the file. What actually stops
"use FortressLibrary for the compiler too" is not codegen at all: it is that
`compile` turns the type checker **on** and `walk` leaves it **off**, and the
interpreter's library has never been through the type checker. When you make
`FortressLibrary` the compiler's prelude, disambiguation passes with **zero**
errors, and then the type checker reports **92 errors** in the library's own
apis and **crashes outright** — `java.lang.Error: Not yet implemented` — on the
`nat`-kinded static parameters the library is built out of. Desugar and codegen
are never reached, in any run, by any variant. So the port is not 108 native
bindings plus a few checker fixes: it is (a) 108 native bindings, (b) a library
type hierarchy that violates the exclusion rules the checker enforces, and
(c) an unimplemented piece of the type checker itself.

---

## 1. Feeding the interpreter prelude to the compiler as it is

The tool did **not** refuse the file, so no renaming was needed
(`02-fortresslibrary-asis.out`):

```
./bin/fortress compile Library/FortressLibrary.fss
File FortressLibrary.fss has 1417 errors.          (exit 255, 2 s)
```

**Phase: DISAMBIGUATE, and only DISAMBIGUATE.** `./bin/fortress disambiguate
Library/FortressLibrary.fss` — which runs the truncated
`PhaseOrder.disambiguatePhaseOrder`, stopping before TYPECHECK — produces
output **byte-identical** to the full compile (`03-disambiguate-only.out`).
Every one of the 1,417 messages comes from
`compiler/disambiguator/TypeDisambiguator.java` (lines 304, 363, 384). The type
checker, the desugarer and the code generator never ran.

**Every error is raised in an `.fsi`, not in the 4,518-line `.fss`.** The
component was never looked at:

| file where the error is raised | errors |
|---|---|
| `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi` | 1,126 |
| `Library/RangeInternals.fsi` | 276 |
| `Library/List.fsi` | 10 |
| `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/NativeArray.fsi` | 2 |
| `Library/FlatString.fsi` | 2 |
| `Library/Stream.fsi` | 1 |

**The 1,417 grouped by kind** (first twenty distinct kinds; the full census is
in `02-fortresslibrary-asis.out`):

| kind | count |
|---|---|
| `Type name may refer to: FortressLibrary.X, CompilerBuiltin.X` / `…, CompilerLibrary.X` | **1,110** |
| `X is undefined.` | **289** |
| `Incorrect number of static arguments for type 'CompilerLibrary.Range': provided 1, expected 0` | **18** |

The 1,110 by colliding name: `ZZ32` 274, `Number` 155, `String` 103,
`Generator` 77, `RR64` 63, `ZZ64` 61, `Range` 51, `TotalComparison` 41,
`Comparison` 41, `NN64` 40, `Matrix` 39, `Reduction` 32, `UncheckedException`
22, `Condition` 21, `ZZ` 15, `CheckedException` 12, `SequentialGenerator` 9,
`LessThan` 9, `GreaterThan` 7, `Unordered` 6, `EqualTo` 6, then 15 more with
≤5 each.

The 289 by missing name: `Integral` 129, `AnyIntegral` 42, `Just` 28, `Char`
14, `Maybe` 10, `OpenRange` 7, `RightRange`/`LeftRange`/`ExtentRange` 6 each,
`BoundedRange` 5, `Indexed` 4, then 19 more with ≤3 each, including `HasRank`,
`Comprehension`, `BigReduction`, `MonoidReduction`, `Array1`,
`ImmutableArray1`, `LexicographicOrder`.

**This number is an artifact, not a finding.** 78% of it is
`FortressLibrary` colliding with `CompilerBuiltin`, because in this run *both*
preludes are in scope: the compiler implicitly imports `CompilerBuiltin` and
`CompilerLibrary` into every compilation unit, and `FortressLibrary` declares
`ZZ32`, `Number`, `String`, `Generator`, … itself. That is what happens when
you compile the interpreter prelude as an *ordinary component*. It is not what
Pavol proposed.

## 2. Pavol's actual proposal: make `FortressLibrary` the prelude

`Shell.useInterpreterLibraries()`, `Shell.setTypeChecking(true)` and
`Shell.setPhaseOrder()` are all public, so the switch `Shell.subMain` flips per
subcommand (`Shell.java:404` vs `421`) can be flipped from outside without
touching a tracked file. `WorldFlip.java` (in this directory) does exactly
that: the **compiler's** phase order — DISAMBIGUATE, TYPECHECK, DESUGAR,
OVERLOADREWRITE, CODEGEN — with the **interpreter's** prelude
(`FortressLibrary` / `FortressBuiltin` / `AnyType`) as the implicit library.

### DISAMBIGUATE: clean

```
java … WorldFlip -stop disambiguate Library/FortressLibrary.fss
### rc=0                                            (05-worldflip-disambiguate.out)
```

Zero errors. All 1,417 disambiguation errors of §1 vanish. The interpreter's
library, its api, and the whole api graph it drags in (`RangeInternals`,
`List`, `NativeArray`, `FlatString`, `Stream`, `String`, `Writer`, `TypeProxy`,
`NatReflect`, `FortressBuiltin`, `AnyType`) resolve names correctly under the
compiler's own disambiguator. **Name resolution is not the problem.**

### TYPECHECK: 92 errors, plus a crash

The full run dies with an uncaught `java.lang.Error: Not yet implemented` from
`STypesUtil.makeInferenceArg` (`04-worldflip-full.out`). To see past the first
casualty, this probe compiles a copy of `compiler/StaticChecker.java` into
`shadow-src/`, prints the name of each compilation unit as it is checked, and
catches the crash instead of letting it abort the pass. The copy is placed
first on the classpath; the tracked file is untouched.

## 2. The rules as built

`pEqv(IntArg, IntArg)` in `TypeAnalyzer.scala` is the plan's table, unchanged:

| left | right | result |
|---|---|---|
| inference variable `$nat$k` | the same variable | true |
| inference variable | anything else `e` | the equality constraint `$nat$k = e` |
| `IntRef n` | `IntRef n` | true |
| `IntRef n` | `IntRef m`, `IntBase 3` | false |
| `IntBase 3` | `IntBase 3` | true; different literals false |
| anything containing `IntBinaryOp` | anything | false; and a *type* that contains arithmetic is refused as ill-formed before that (but see § 3 for where the well-formedness check does not reach) |

The equality track is solved exactly as the op track is: cliques from `getEquality`, unified in
`un`, with a clique that holds two different sizes, or anything that is not a symbol or a
literal, having no unifier. `reduce`'s nat twin refuses a variable constrained to two different
sizes, and `neg` has a nat branch so that negation stays total.

**Decision E2, concretely.** There is no `killNatIvars` and no default to 0. An unsolved nat
variable is simply left in place; `hasInferenceVars` was extended to find one, so an unknown
size that reaches a **type** is reported by the existing "not enough context" path
(`impls/Functionals.scala:248-250`), and one that reaches nothing is never looked at. That is
why the api's dead sizes pass: their parameters occur in no domain, no range and no body, so no
constraint about them is ever generated and no entry for them ever enters the solver.

The plan says six such declarations at `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1508-1523`. Measured, the
api has **25** declarations with at least one dead size, and the six with a dead `nat m, nat p`
are at `:1511, :1514, :1517, :1520, :1523, :1526` — the plan's line range is three lines early
and stops one short. The others: a dead `nat o` in the three `subarray` methods (`:1401`,
`:1423`, `:1451`) and two dead offsets in the 2-D one (`:1562`); a dead `nat m` in three vector
operators (`:1499-1505`); a dead `nat p` in eight matrix operators (`:1624-1646`); and a dead
`nat n` in four traits whose parameter is part of their identity (`:1068, :1089, :1091, :1093`).
Under E1 (default to 0) or E3 (delete them) the library edit would be 25 declarations, not six.

**What is deliberately not in.** The `checkP` relaxation of
`perf-probes/prelude/exclusion-trace.md` § 5 (landed 2026-09-21) is not here, so the library's
exclusion errors stay and the before/after counts are comparable. Exclusion between two nat
literals is also untouched (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:447-451`, "Todo: Handle int, nat, bool args"):
an overload set distinguished only by two sizes is still rejected as ambiguous, the
conservative side, and the team wanted it allowed (`internal-document.tex:183-198`). `bool`,
`dim` and `unit` get a named checker error, not rules. `where`-clause `NatConstraint`s and
`requires` contracts are untouched.

== explorations/perf-probes/nat/REPORT.md:171-235

## 3. The probes (§ e step 2)

All in the **compiler's own world** — `CompilerLibrary` as the prelude — compiled into a private
cache that the shadow built from scratch in library order. Capture: `01-probes-shadow.out`;
`pNat1`'s run-time failure in full: `01b-pNat1-run-stack.out`.

| probe | what it is | `fortress compile` | `fortress run` |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pNat1.fss` (prelude probe) | `unbox[\nat k\](b: Box[\k\])`, the nat **inferred** from the argument type | **exit=0**, no error | `NoClassDefFoundError: 3$RTTIc` |
| `pNat2.fss` (prelude probe) | the same with `unbox[\3\](…)` written out | **exit=0**, no error | `NoClassDefFoundError: 3$RTTIc` |
| `pNat3.fss` (prelude probe) | the type-parameter control | exit=0 | `7` |
| `pNat4.fss` | the deliberate mismatch `unbox[\4\](Box[\3\](7))` | **1 error**: `[\4\]Box[\4\]->ZZ32 is not applicable to an argument of type Box[\3\]` | — |
| `pNat5.fss` | arithmetic in a declared type, `b: Box[\k + 1\]` | **2 errors**: `Ill-formed type: Box[\k+1\] / Arithmetic on nat static arguments is not checked; use a nat parameter or a literal.`, and the call then does not apply | — |
| `pNat6.fss` | arithmetic in a static argument at the use site, `Box[\2 + 1\](7)` | **1 error**, but a different one: `[\3\]Box[\3\]->ZZ32 is not applicable to an argument of type Box[\2+1\]` | — |
| `pNatVec.fss` | the specification's `makeVector` shape: one nat in the parameter list and the return type, explicit instantiation, the size inferred at a call, the size in value position | **exit=0**, no error | `NoClassDefFoundError: 3$RTTIc` |
| `pNatBool.fss` | a `bool` static parameter | **1 error**: `Static argument inference for the bool static parameter b is not supported by the type checker.` | — |

So the checker half of § e step 2 is green on every line of it, including the two refusals, and
including the case the plan expected to need bug (i) found (`pNat2`) — which it did.

Three notes.

**The specification's own example could not be run as it stands.** `SpecData/examples/basic/StatParam.Nat.fss`
is `makeVector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]():Vector[\T,s0\] = vector[\T,s0\]`, and `Vector`,
`vector` and `Number` are all the *interpreter* library's; the compiler's prelude has none of
them (its one nat-parameterized declaration is the deliberately empty
`trait Matrix[\T, nat s0, nat s1\]` at `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:512`). `pNatVec.fss`
reproduces the shape over a local carrier and says so in a comment.

**Where the two paths really differ is narrower than the plan says.** The plan expects the
refusal of arithmetic to be the one place the compiled and interpreted paths diverge. Measured
on the interpreter (`07-interpreter-arithmetic.out`), `pNat5` — arithmetic in a *declared*
parameter type — is refused by the **interpreter too**:
`Unification error: Cannot unify Box[\4\] … with Box[\k+1\]`, because
`IntNat.unifyStaticArg` (`interpreter/evaluator/types/IntNat.java:127-147`) does a literal
comparison, a symbol binding, or an error, and an `IntBinaryOp` is none of those. The
divergence is `pNat6`: arithmetic in a static argument written at the *use* site, `Box[\2 + 1\]`,
which `EvalType.forIntArg` (`interpreter/evaluator/EvalType.java:431-464`) evaluates to the
type `Box[\nat 3\]` — the interpreter prints `7`, and the shadow refuses it. So the minimal
design costs exactly one shape: a computed static argument at a use site, which no program in
the census writes.

It refuses it, though, with the wrong message, and that is a gap in the shadow worth naming.
The well-formedness check on arithmetic lives in `TypeWellFormedChecker`'s `STraitType` case,
so it fires on a *type* that contains arithmetic (`pNat5`, `Ill-formed type: Box[\k+1\]`) but

`ExportChecker.equalIntExprs` is `= false` with the comment "Not implemented!" in the tree
(`scala_src/typechecker/ExportChecker.scala:645-648`), so *every* exported signature whose types
carry a nat static argument fails the export check — the api and the component are declared
identically and the checker says they differ. The probes never reached that far before, because
the checker crashed first.

`pNatExp.fsi` / `pNatExp.fss` is the library's shape in miniature: `mk` and `len` declared
identically in api and component, their types carrying a nat static argument (`Vec[\T,s\]`), and
`opr DOT[\T, nat n, nat m\]` in the api against `opr DOT[\T, nat n\]` in the component — the
shape of `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1511-1527` against `.fss:2264-2280`. The A/B is one build:
`-Dprobe.nat.exportAsTree=true` puts the tree's answer back. Capture: `05-exportchecker.out`.

|---|---|

| structural (`Formula.nEq`) | **1** missing declaration: `DOT[\T extends Object,nat n,nat m\](a:Vec[\T,n\],b:Vec[\T,n\]):ZZ32` |

**Decision F question 2, answered.** Under E2 the export checker reports the dead-size
declaration, and it reports it as *the api declares something the component does not define* —
not through `equalIntExprs` at all, but through `equalListStaticParams`
(`ExportChecker.scala:613-627`), which compares the parameter lists by length, name and kind, so
`[\T, nat n, nat m\]` and `[\T, nat n\]` differ before any type is looked at. The message names
the api's declaration and its line. The six operators of the library (and the eight matrix ones,
and the four `subarray` methods) will each produce one such line — an *ordinary error at the
api*, not a crash, and not silence. E3 (delete the dead parameters) is what makes it go away;
E2 in the checker does not, and was never meant to.

## 2. The rules as built

`pEqv(IntArg, IntArg)` in `TypeAnalyzer.scala` is the plan's table, unchanged:

| left | right | result |
|---|---|---|
| inference variable `$nat$k` | the same variable | true |
| inference variable | anything else `e` | the equality constraint `$nat$k = e` |
| `IntRef n` | `IntRef n` | true |
| `IntRef n` | `IntRef m`, `IntBase 3` | false |
| `IntBase 3` | `IntBase 3` | true; different literals false |
| anything containing `IntBinaryOp` | anything | false; and a *type* that contains arithmetic is refused as ill-formed before that (but see § 3 for where the well-formedness check does not reach) |

The equality track is solved exactly as the op track is: cliques from `getEquality`, unified in
`un`, with a clique that holds two different sizes, or anything that is not a symbol or a
literal, having no unifier. `reduce`'s nat twin refuses a variable constrained to two different
sizes, and `neg` has a nat branch so that negation stays total.

**Decision E2, concretely.** There is no `killNatIvars` and no default to 0. An unsolved nat
variable is simply left in place; `hasInferenceVars` was extended to find one, so an unknown
size that reaches a **type** is reported by the existing "not enough context" path
(`impls/Functionals.scala:248-250`), and one that reaches nothing is never looked at. That is
why the api's dead sizes pass: their parameters occur in no domain, no range and no body, so no
constraint about them is ever generated and no entry for them ever enters the solver.

The plan says six such declarations at `Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1508-1523`. Measured, the
api has **25** declarations with at least one dead size, and the six with a dead `nat m, nat p`
are at `:1511, :1514, :1517, :1520, :1523, :1526` — the plan's line range is three lines early
and stops one short. The others: a dead `nat o` in the three `subarray` methods (`:1401`,
`:1423`, `:1451`) and two dead offsets in the 2-D one (`:1562`); a dead `nat m` in three vector
operators (`:1499-1505`); a dead `nat p` in eight matrix operators (`:1624-1646`); and a dead
`nat n` in four traits whose parameter is part of their identity (`:1068, :1089, :1091, :1093`).
Under E1 (default to 0) or E3 (delete them) the library edit would be 25 declarations, not six.

**What is deliberately not in.** The `checkP` relaxation of
`perf-probes/prelude/exclusion-trace.md` § 5 (landed 2026-09-21) is not here, so the library's
exclusion errors stay and the before/after counts are comparable. Exclusion between two nat
literals is also untouched (`TypeAnalyzer.scala:447-451`, "Todo: Handle int, nat, bool args"):
an overload set distinguished only by two sizes is still rejected as ambiguous, the
conservative side, and the team wanted it allowed (`internal-document.tex:183-198`). `bool`,
`dim` and `unit` get a named checker error, not rules. `where`-clause `NatConstraint`s and
`requires` contracts are untouched.

## 5. What the library already does with sizes

- The sized traits: `Array1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]`, `Vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]`, `Array2`, `Matrix[\T extends Number, nat s0, nat s1\]`, `Array3` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1440, 1465, 1542, 1583, 1657`).
- Shared sizes in the products: `opr DOT[\T extends Number, nat n, nat m, nat p\](me: Matrix[\T,n,m\], other: Matrix[\T,m,p\]): Matrix[\T,n,p\]` (`.fsi:1619-1620`) and the vector forms (`.fsi:1513-1530`). Every `DOT` arm is generic in its sizes, so the family is an overload set of size-generic arms.
  - Revised 2026-09-24 after the size probes: that shape was measured on row 214's three arms. A answers with the catch-all and B answers right (§ 2).
  - `DOT`'s shared `m`, the same size in two arguments, is not probed under either design (§ 12).
- Literals: 4 distinct size literals (0, 1, 2, 3) written as static arguments in 85 places, 78 of them `0`; 244 nat parameters declared (`runtime/r7-lib-literals.txt`). Under B that is four holder classes for the library's own literals. Under A it is one descriptor class and interface per sized type used.
- Dead sizes: 25 api declarations carry a size that occurs in no domain, range or body (`REPORT.md` § 2). The checker lets them pass by decision E2 (POSITIONS:47). Neither design meets them unless a dead size reaches a name (`REPORT.md` § 11).
- Sizes read as numbers inside sized traits: `getter size():ZZ32 = s0` and `opr |self| : ZZ32 = s0` in `ReadableArray1` (`FortressLibrary.fss:2022, 2036`); `s0 s1` in `Array2` (`:2299, 2320`); `s0 s1 s2` in `Array3` (`:2680, 2712`); `o::m#s` and `o-b0` in `subarray` (`:2127-2128`). Revised 2026-09-24 after the size probes: the trait-getter shape was measured as `NatGetter`. It needs A's 7-line fourth-gap piece and prints 3 under both designs (`size-probes.md` § 3).
- Sizes in `extends` clauses: `trait Rank1 extends { Rank[\1\]}` and its two siblings (`.fss:1605-1611`). These are three of the five library declarations the checker passes clean and the code generator refuses (`perf-probes/prelude/desugar-codegen.md`, "The five"). Design A's one `continue` is the branch they reach (measured on `NatExtends2`, which writes a symbol; the literal case is by reading). Revised 2026-09-24 after the size probes: under B, `extends-b.patch` (14 lines) pushes a symbol's field or a literal's holder, measured with a symbol on `NatExtends1`, `NatGetter` and `pNatDispTrait`.

### 2.4 What design A would need, not built

The brief's condition was "reading a size out of the value's descriptor class name". The dispatcher needs more than that under A. By reading:

1. **Finding the stem.** Every sized descriptor interface carries its size in its name (`Vec❮3❯$RTTIi`, `CodeGen.java:5227`), and so does its supertype list (`:5249`). A value reaches a trait arm through its object's descriptor: the template is `interface Arr1❮s❯$RTTIi extends Vctr❮s❯$RTTIi`, stamped at `❮3❯` (`s1b-javap.txt:34-38`). The dispatcher cannot name that interface in an `INSTANCEOF`. It needs a run-time helper that walks the value's descriptor class and its interfaces, matches the stem by name, and returns the sizes. About 20 lines in `RTHelpers`.
2. **The other arguments of that stem.** The type-argument getters are named per size too (`Arr1❮s❯__1`, `Vec❮3❯__1`; `CodeGen.java:5267`; `s1b-javap.txt:37, 53`). Checking `RR64` in `Vctr[\RR64,s\]` needs reflection, about 8 lines, or a size-free interface per sized stem, which is a change to A's naming.
3. **The inference loop.** It keeps each static argument as a descriptor in a local and compares repeated occurrences with `runtimeSupertypeOf` (`OverloadSet.java:1410-1636`). A size would be a string there. Storing it and comparing it by equality is about 10 lines. The library's `DOT` shares a size between two arguments (`FortressLibrary.fsi:1619-1620`), so the comparison is needed.
4. **The closure loader.** `RTHelpers.loadClosureClass` takes `RTTI[]`, hashes `getSN()` and names the class from `className()` (`runtimeSystem/RTHelpers.java:160-178`). A size needs a variant that takes a string, about 12 lines, plus about 5 lines at the emitted call (`OverloadSet.java:1637-1696`). The alternative is a descriptor object made at dispatch, which is B's `RTTIsize` inside A.
5. **Recognising the size variable** in `makeTypeStructure` and a new structure kind to emit 1-2: about 15-25 lines.

About 70-90 lines in `OverloadSet` and `RTHelpers`, not built. Two questions in it are Pavol's:

- **How does a size travel inside the dispatcher and into the closure loader?** As a string beside the descriptor objects, a second channel through the loader's API. Or as a descriptor object made at dispatch, which is design B's object used by design A.
- **How does the dispatcher reach a sized stem's descriptor interface and getters, whose names hold the size?** By reflection at every dispatch. Or by giving each sized stem a size-free interface, which adds to A's naming what B's descriptor already has.

## 5. What the library already does with sizes

- The sized traits: `Array1[\T, nat b0, nat s0\]`, `Vector[\T extends Number, nat s0\]`, `Array2`, `Matrix[\T extends Number, nat s0, nat s1\]`, `Array3` (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1440, 1465, 1542, 1583, 1657`).
- Shared sizes in the products: `opr DOT[\T extends Number, nat n, nat m, nat p\](me: Matrix[\T,n,m\], other: Matrix[\T,m,p\]): Matrix[\T,n,p\]` (`.fsi:1619-1620`) and the vector forms (`.fsi:1513-1530`). Every `DOT` arm is generic in its sizes, so the family is an overload set of size-generic arms.
  - Revised 2026-09-24 after the size probes: that shape was measured on row 214's three arms. A answers with the catch-all and B answers right (§ 2).
  - `DOT`'s shared `m`, the same size in two arguments, is not probed under either design (§ 12).
- Literals: 4 distinct size literals (0, 1, 2, 3) written as static arguments in 85 places, 78 of them `0`; 244 nat parameters declared (`runtime/r7-lib-literals.txt`). Under B that is four holder classes for the library's own literals. Under A it is one descriptor class and interface per sized type used.
- Dead sizes: 25 api declarations carry a size that occurs in no domain, range or body (`REPORT.md` § 2). The checker lets them pass by decision E2 (POSITIONS:47). Neither design meets them unless a dead size reaches a name (`REPORT.md` § 11).
- Sizes read as numbers inside sized traits: `getter size():ZZ32 = s0` and `opr |self| : ZZ32 = s0` in `ReadableArray1` (`FortressLibrary.fss:2022, 2036`); `s0 s1` in `Array2` (`:2299, 2320`); `s0 s1 s2` in `Array3` (`:2680, 2712`); `o::m#s` and `o-b0` in `subarray` (`:2127-2128`). Revised 2026-09-24 after the size probes: the trait-getter shape was measured as `NatGetter`. It needs A's 7-line fourth-gap piece and prints 3 under both designs (`size-probes.md` § 3).
- Sizes in `extends` clauses: `trait Rank1 extends { Rank[\1\]}` and its two siblings (`.fss:1605-1611`). These are three of the five library declarations the checker passes clean and the code generator refuses (`perf-probes/prelude/desugar-codegen.md`, "The five"). Design A's one `continue` is the branch they reach (measured on `NatExtends2`, which writes a symbol; the literal case is by reading). Revised 2026-09-24 after the size probes: under B, `extends-b.patch` (14 lines) pushes a symbol's field or a literal's holder, measured with a symbol on `NatExtends1`, `NatGetter` and `pNatDispTrait`.
- Arithmetic in sizes: the storing objects' `PrimitiveArray[\T, (s0 s1)\]` (`.fss:2423, 2571, 2794`) and `reflect`'s `__refl'[\r+b, b+b\]` (`NatReflect.fss:42-48`). The first rung refuses arithmetic (`array-design-review.md`, Serious 5); neither design evaluates it.
- Where the team departed: the compiler world's one numeric array, `ZZ32Vector`, has no size parameter and keeps its shape as four integers in the Java object (`LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi:563`; `compiler/runtimeValues/FZZ32Vector.java:18-19`; `coordinator/array-design.md` § 2), the X10 and Fortran way. The compiler prelude's only sized declaration is an empty `trait Matrix[\T, nat s0, nat s1\]` (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fss:638`), deleted at the switch-over (POSITIONS:46). The interpreter's library makes sizes as types at run time (`reflect`), B's shape at the interpreter.

### 2.4 What design A would need, not built

The brief's condition was "reading a size out of the value's descriptor class name". The dispatcher needs more than that under A. By reading:

1. **Finding the stem.** Every sized descriptor interface carries its size in its name (`Vec❮3❯$RTTIi`, `CodeGen.java:5227`), and so does its supertype list (`:5249`). A value reaches a trait arm through its object's descriptor: the template is `interface Arr1❮s❯$RTTIi extends Vctr❮s❯$RTTIi`, stamped at `❮3❯` (`s1b-javap.txt:34-38`). The dispatcher cannot name that interface in an `INSTANCEOF`. It needs a run-time helper that walks the value's descriptor class and its interfaces, matches the stem by name, and returns the sizes. About 20 lines in `RTHelpers`.
2. **The other arguments of that stem.** The type-argument getters are named per size too (`Arr1❮s❯__1`, `Vec❮3❯__1`; `CodeGen.java:5267`; `s1b-javap.txt:37, 53`). Checking `RR64` in `Vctr[\RR64,s\]` needs reflection, about 8 lines, or a size-free interface per sized stem, which is a change to A's naming.
3. **The inference loop.** It keeps each static argument as a descriptor in a local and compares repeated occurrences with `runtimeSupertypeOf` (`OverloadSet.java:1410-1636`). A size would be a string there. Storing it and comparing it by equality is about 10 lines. The library's `DOT` shares a size between two arguments (`FortressLibrary.fsi:1619-1620`), so the comparison is needed.
4. **The closure loader.** `RTHelpers.loadClosureClass` takes `RTTI[]`, hashes `getSN()` and names the class from `className()` (`runtimeSystem/RTHelpers.java:160-178`). A size needs a variant that takes a string, about 12 lines, plus about 5 lines at the emitted call (`OverloadSet.java:1637-1696`). The alternative is a descriptor object made at dispatch, which is B's `RTTIsize` inside A.
5. **Recognising the size variable** in `makeTypeStructure` and a new structure kind to emit 1-2: about 15-25 lines.

About 70-90 lines in `OverloadSet` and `RTHelpers`, not built. Two questions in it are Pavol's:

- **How does a size travel inside the dispatcher and into the closure loader?** As a string beside the descriptor objects, a second channel through the loader's API. Or as a descriptor object made at dispatch, which is design B's object used by design A.
- **How does the dispatcher reach a sized stem's descriptor interface and getters, whose names hold the size?** By reflection at every dispatch. Or by giving each sized stem a size-free interface, which adds to A's naming what B's descriptor already has.

**The programs.**

- `pTypeCase2.fss`: its type-parameter control.

| program | design A | design B | walk | capture |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `pTypeCase2` | three four other | three four other | same | `s3-typecase.out:2-7`; `:26-31` |
| `pNatCase2` | three four other other | three four other other | same | `:9-15`; `:33-39` |
| `pNatCaseGen` | yes no no yes | yes no no yes | same | `:17-23`; `:41-47` |

- The test is an `INSTANCEOF` on the value's own class under both designs: `Vec⟦FZZ32,3⟧`, then `Vec⟦FZZ32,4⟧` (`s3b-javap.txt:6, 14`). In the generic function's template it is `INSTANCEOF Vec⟦FZZ32,s⟧` (`:30`), and the loader fills in the size when it stamps `isOfSize⟦3⟧` and `isOfSize⟦4⟧`.
- The descriptor is not consulted, so the choice of design does not enter.

(* See explorations/compile-ladder/rung-size-runtime/REPORT.md. *)
component NatRtCaseGen
export Executable
object Vec[\T, nat s\](x: T) end
isOfSize[\nat s\](v: Any): String =
  typecase v of
    Vec[\ZZ32,s\] => "yes"
    else => "no"
  end
run() = do
  a: Any = Vec[\ZZ32,3\](7)
  println(isOfSize[\3\](a))
  println(isOfSize[\4\](a))
  b: Any = Vec[\ZZ32,4\](7)
  println(isOfSize[\3\](b))
  println(isOfSize[\4\](b))
end
end

101	`fortress compile` runs the same phases with the static type checker, in Scala, switched on. Before the checker, it folds integer literals. After the phases, the code generator writes JVM bytecode into a jar. A type error stops the compile.
102	
103	Each path has its own library today. At the switch-over, the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, and the compiler's prelude, three files of its library, is deleted (`references/compiler.md`). The switch-over comes when the checker accepts the interpreter's library.
104	
105	### The compiled run time
106	
107	`fortress run` compiles no Fortress source. It runs the jars of the program and of the library on the JVM. A jar holds JVM class files:
108	
109	- the component's functions, objects and traits;
110	- its closures;
111	- one dispatch method for each overloaded name. It tests the run-time types of all the arguments, from the most specific declaration to the least specific. Walk also chooses at run time.
112	
113	A generic declaration is compiled once, as a template class. The first time that a program uses an instantiation, such as `Box[\RR64\]`, the class loader makes its class. It copies the template's bytecode, puts in the static arguments, and loads the result. A static argument is a type, or a size as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`. These classes are never on disk. C# specialises generics in this way. Java erases them.
114	
115	The class loader is code of this tree that the revival changes, so a failure while a class loads can be its defect (`references/compiler.md`).
116	
117	HotSpot, the JVM's compiler, then compiles the hot bytecode to machine code. A number is a boxed object, also inside a specialised class: `RR64` is the class `FRR64`. An array is a library object, read and written through its `get` and `put` methods.

`fortress compile` runs the same phases with the static type checker, in Scala, switched on. Before the checker, it folds integer literals. After the phases, the code generator writes JVM bytecode into a jar. A type error stops the compile.

Each path has its own library today. At the switch-over, the compiled path moves onto the interpreter's library, and the compiler's prelude, three files of its library, is deleted (`references/compiler.md`). The switch-over comes when the checker accepts the interpreter's library.

### The compiled run time

`fortress run` compiles no Fortress source. It runs the jars of the program and of the library on the JVM. A jar holds JVM class files:

- the component's functions, objects and traits;
- its closures;
- one dispatch method for each overloaded name. It tests the run-time types of all the arguments, from the most specific declaration to the least specific. Walk also chooses at run time.

A generic declaration is compiled once, as a template class. The first time that a program uses an instantiation, such as `Box[\RR64\]`, the class loader makes its class. It copies the template's bytecode, puts in the static arguments, and loads the result. A static argument is a type, or a size as a descriptor from `RTTIsize.of`. These classes are never on disk. C# specialises generics in this way. Java erases them.

The class loader is code of this tree that the revival changes, so a failure while a class loads can be its defect (`references/compiler.md`).

HotSpot, the JVM's compiler, then compiles the hot bytecode to machine code. A number is a boxed object, also inside a specialised class: `RR64` is the class `FRR64`. An array is a library object, read and written through its `get` and `put` methods.

### The caches

A run keeps the results of its phases in the caches, so that a later run can reuse them. The caches are folders in `default_repository/caches/`, or in a private caches folder that a run names. An entry is one file in a cache, written for one source file.

- `interpreter_parsed_cache/`: walk's parsed tree of each file, `X-<hash>.tfi` for an api and `X-<hash>.tfs` for a component.
- `interpreter_cache/`: walk's tree of each component after the phases. Walk loads it back and interprets it. The entry is a text dump of the tree. It starts `(Component @"/home/user/fortress/Library/FlatString.fss":12:1~156:2 ...`.

- F-25 **On the compiled path, the class loader loads each class under the JDK's class-loading lock, so the first load of an instantiation's class is safe on four threads at once.** `InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` holds `getClassLoadingLock(name)` for the whole load, as the JDK's own `ClassLoader.loadClass` does. Without the lock, two threads that first loaded such classes at the same time could race, and the run died with a `NullPointerException` (row 417, fixed). The test `compiler_tests/FirstLoadThreadsRungG` calls a generic overload at eight instances in a parallel `for` loop. Observed: at four threads it failed 5 runs of 5 before the lock, and passed 5 of 5 after. It is one of the gate's atomic runs, which run each program at four threads (`gate.md`). Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-generic-runtime/REPORT.md` sections 1 (the runs) and 12 (why this lock).
- F-26 **Under walk, when one of two applicable declarations has static parameters of its own, the call chooses on their declared domains where exactly one lies inside the other, not by the order in which they are written.** This is walk's half of P-45, the rule that a call chooses among overloads by the parameter types that each declares. A declaration has static parameters of its own if it is a generic function or constructor, or a functional method with static parameters in a trait or object without any. Its declared domain is its parameter types, each type parameter standing for itself under its bounds: walk's symbolic instance of it. Where neither declared domain lies inside the other, or neither declaration has static parameters of its own, walk compares the domains of the instances that the call makes. So a functional method of a generic trait or object is compared on its instance; a generic dotted method follows F-253. If the chosen instance takes an argument only by a conversion, walk converts the argument and dispatches again, so the most specific declaration for the converted values runs. It keeps the first choice for an overloaded method, and where `Coercions.coercionFor` finds no conversion for an argument, such as a tuple converted element by element. Two generic overloads whose static parameters agree in name, kind and bounds share one symbolic instance, even if their `where` clauses differ; no test or library declaration has such a pair (row 478). Gated by `tests/DispatchDeclaredDomain.fss` and `DispatchConvertedAgain.fss`; the code is `OverloadedFunction.moreSpecificDeclaration` and `convertedCall`. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.1 (the choice), 5.2 (the second dispatch) and 5.5 (the symbolic instance).
- F-27 **Walk's load check accepts two kinds of overload pair that its parameter-by-parameter check refuses: a generic declaration beside a plain one, read on their declared domains, and two plain declarations whose overlap other declarations cover through `comprises` clauses.** The load check is walk's check of each overload set as the program loads. It reads a pair in these ways only after the parameter-by-parameter check refuses it. To test a cover, it cuts the overlap of the two domains, position by position, into parts by the `comprises` clauses. Each combination of parts must lie inside the domain of one declaration without static parameters that lies below both. So several such declarations may together cover the overlap. A search that does not settle refuses. A generic declaration beside a plain one needs the same cover where neither declared domain lies inside the other. This is walk's half of P-46, the choice on declared parameter types, and of P-60, which lets several declarations below both cover a meet. Two generic declarations are read on their declared domains too, by the same rules (F-252); walk still refuses the POPL 2019 paper's valid example, a set of three generic declarations (row 539). Gated by `tests/ComprisesMeetWalk.fss` and `GenericBesidePlain*.fss`, among others. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-dispatch/REPORT.md` sections 5.3 (generic beside plain) and 5.4 (the cover).
- F-29 **Under walk, the load check refuses a trait or object that extends a closed trait of the program's main component where the trait's `comprises` clause does not allow it.** A closed trait is one with a `comprises` clause. The check reads every trait and object of the program as a possible extender. An extender is allowed if it lies below a listed type, or if it is a trait that is closed or generic in the ways that the specification allows (`Specification/basic/traits.tex`, "Trait Declarations"). The check does not yet read a clause declared outside the main component, the library's among them (row 551), or an object expression's `extends` clause (row 597). Nor does it check that each listed type extends the trait at every instantiation (row 598). Two breaches wait for a check that reads the library's clauses: the library's `Reflect` (row 595), and team tests that extend `Number` or `Exception` directly (row 596). Gated by `tests/ComprisesUnlistedExtender` and `ComprisesGenericChildUnlistedExtender`, refused at load, and by the `XXX` tests of rows 487, 551, 597 and 598, which stay green while walk still loads their programs. Detail: `compile-ladder/rung-walk-load-check/REPORT.md` section 5.
- F-32 **The compiled path cannot reuse walk's glue classes, the Java classes that the one library's native bindings name; at `e455ccd98` (2026-09-29) the library had 424 such bindings.** A native binding is a library body `builtinPrimitive("…")`; its string names a glue class, which takes walk's boxed values. The compiled path calls static helpers over plain Java values instead, in `nativeHelpers/`. Matched against those helpers, the 424 bindings were: 147 that need only a new text (P-58 gives the text); 61 with a helper that nothing binds, 25 of them under a name that the compiler's prelude gives to another helper, such as the 12 wrapping operators (row 348); 138 that need a new helper; and 78 that need more, 36 methods of native I/O objects and 42 with no compiled analogue. The count leaves out the five `IntLiteral` conversion bindings, `asZZ32` to `asZZ` in `FortressBuiltin.fss`, added on 2026-10-02. Every program's output needs `Writer`'s natives, since `println` writes through a native `Writer`. MicroGPT also needs `nanoTime`, which needs a new helper, since the compiled one returns `RR64`; `getProgramArgsPrim`, which `System` calls as it loads; and `NativeArray`. The last two have no compiled analogue. PLAN phase 4, "The natives", moves the bindings onto helpers; the 42 with no analogue wait, `NativeArray` for the array decision on how a float vector's `double[]` store goes (P-85). Detail: `perf-probes/prelude/natives-shape.md` section 2, which classes each binding.
- F-34 **In single measurements of September 2026, only the checker stood between the interpreter's library and bytecode: disambiguation, desugaring and code generation refused almost nothing that the checker passed.** With `FortressLibrary` as the compiled path's prelude, disambiguation reported no error (2026-09-16, `perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md` section 2). With the checker's failures caught per declaration, desugaring and the overload rewriting reported none (2026-09-20, `perf-probes/prelude/desugar-codegen.md` section 4.2). On 2026-09-27, on the library at `2851e5086`, after its number types became siblings, code generation on `FortressLibrary.fss` emitted 326 declarations and refused 225. Only 4 of the 225 were declarations that the checker passed: two `AsIfExpr`, one `LetFn` and one call on a receiver of intersection type. The other 221 were declarations that the checker failed on, and overloads that the overload rewriting made. The dispatch generator refused 12 of 198 overload sets, each a functional method and a top-level function with one signature. The gate's distance stage does not run code generation, so nothing has measured it since. Compiled as an ordinary component, beside the compiler's own prelude, the library gave 1,417 disambiguation errors: an artifact of the two preludes in scope at once (`perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md` section 1). Detail: `perf-probes/prelude/switch-over-distance-flat.md` sections 3 (code generation) and 4 (the dispatch generator).
- F-35 **The `FortressLibrary` api has 8 declarations with a dead size: a size parameter that occurs in none of the declaration's parameter types, return type or body.** They are the three one-dimensional `subarray` methods, with `nat o`; the two-dimensional `subarray`, with `nat o0` and `nat o1`; and the traits `Rank`, `Indexed1`, `Indexed2` and `Indexed3`, whose `nat n` is part of the type's identity. They check clean, since a size that reaches no type, name or value is no error (P-40). There were 25 when they were counted on 2026-09-21; the 17 vector and matrix operators have lost theirs since (P-40). A diff that removes the other 8 waits for the curator, with the switch-over's design (review-queue item 36; PLAN item 12). Where a component declares a function without the api's dead size, the export checker reports the api's declaration as missing, since it compares static-parameter lists by length, name and kind. Detail: `perf-probes/nat/REPORT.md` sections 2 (the 25, by line) and 7 (the export checker).

The test `compiler_tests/FirstLoadThreadsRungG` calls a generic overload at eight instances in a parallel `for` loop.
